title: Endometrial Polyps: Update Overview on Etiology, Diagnosis, Natural History and Treatment
clinical_background: Endometrial polyps are localized projections of the uterine lining formed by overgrowth of endometrial glands and stroma around a vascular core. Most are benign, but atypical hyperplasia or endometrial carcinoma may be present in 3.8% of postmenopausal patients. Abnormal uterine bleeding is reported in 3.7–65% of patients diagnosed with polyps; other polyps are found incidentally in asymptomatic women. They may also be associated with infertility and recurrent miscarriage in younger women.
objectives: Provide an updated overview of the literature on the pathophysiology, natural history, diagnosis and treatment of endometrial polyps.
study_design: Literature review covering the pathophysiology, natural history, diagnosis, and treatment of endometrial polyps.
main_conclusion: The authors conclude that this literature overview may help clinicians update their knowledge of endometrial polyp management.
narrative_summary:
This review surveys the pathophysiology, natural history, diagnosis and treatment of endometrial polyps. These lesions are often asymptomatic, but may be associated with abnormal uterine bleeding and infertility. Their estimated prevalence varies from 7.8% to 34.9% across populations and risk profiles. Polyps may regress, persist or enlarge; a cited study reported spontaneous regression in 26.7% of cases after 1 year of follow-up among polyps with a mean diameter of 10.7 mm. Malignancy risk warrants consideration: a cited systematic review of 9266 women estimated that endometrial cancer confined to a polyp occurred in 3.1%, with rates of 1.12% in premenopausal women and 4.93% in postmenopausal women.

Transvaginal ultrasound has reported sensitivity of 91% and specificity of 90%, while diagnostic hysteroscopy is considered the diagnostic gold standard and permits direct assessment and removal. Blind biopsy or curettage is discouraged because of its low sensitivity and the possibility of missing malignant cells at the polyp base. Management should account for symptoms, pregnancy plans, malignancy risk and procedural considerations. Expectant management can be considered for asymptomatic premenopausal patients with small polyps (≤1 cm) and low carcinoma risk, following counseling about that risk. Hysteroscopic polypectomy is described as an effective conservative treatment, although recurrence after complete removal ranges from approximately 2.5% to 43.6%. Hysterectomy is not considered first-line treatment.
interpretation: Endometrial polyps vary in presentation and clinical course: they may regress, persist, enlarge or contain premalignant or malignant changes. Larger polyps appear less likely to regress spontaneously. Malignancy risk warrants attention, particularly in postmenopausal women and those with abnormal uterine bleeding, although the evidence does not establish that polyps themselves are precursors of endometrial cancer. Hysteroscopy provides direct assessment and permits removal, while management can be individualized.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: A cited prospective study supported the observation that polyps larger than 1 cm tend to persist and cause abnormal uterine bleeding more often than smaller polyps. Prior studies disagree about whether polyp size predicts atypical histology or cancer: some found no influence, whereas others reported more atypical findings with diameters greater than 15 and 18 mm. A cited retrospective study of 1467 patients interpreted polyps as incidental findings rather than precursors of endometrial cancer. The authors also report evidence from a systematic review suggesting improved clinical pregnancy rates after hysteroscopic polypectomy before ARTs, while noting that a causal relationship between polyps and infertility remains unestablished.
clinical_implications: Most endometrial polyps are asymptomatic, but they may be associated with abnormal uterine bleeding or infertility.

Postmenopausal status and abnormal uterine bleeding are presented as major predictors of endometrial cancer in patients with polyps; the cited meta-analysis reported respective relative risks of 3.86 (95% CI 2.92–5.11) and 1.97 (95% CI 1.24–3.15).
Transvaginal ultrasound findings are not specific to polyps and may resemble submucosal leiomyomas, endometrial hyperplasia or endometrial cancer.
Hysterosonography can improve lesion detection and characterization compared with conventional transvaginal ultrasound, but cannot provide a definitive histopathological diagnosis or treatment.

Hysteroscopic polypectomy is described as effective and safe, with symptomatic relief reported for 75 to 100% of patients; recurrence after complete excision is reported in approximately 2.5% to 43.6% of cases.
practice_implications: Individualize management according to pregnancy plans, symptoms, malignancy risk factors and the clinician’s technical expertise; the options described are observation, conservative surgery and radical surgery.

Observation can be considered for asymptomatic premenopausal patients with small polyps (≤1 cm) and low endometrial carcinoma risk. The cited AAGL guidelines advise counseling about the potential carcinoma risk before offering this approach.
Use hysteroscopy as the diagnostic reference standard when assessing endometrial polyps; it permits direct characterization and may allow diagnosis and removal in one outpatient procedure.

During hysteroscopy, document polyp number, size, location relative to the tubal ostium, texture, implantation base, superficial vessels and coexisting pathology. Abundant, tortuous superficial vessels are highlighted as the most relevant hysteroscopic feature raising suspicion of malignancy.
Do not substitute Doppler or power Doppler ultrasonography for histopathological assessment after surgical removal: the authors state that supporting evidence is insufficient.

Blind biopsy or curettage is discouraged for polyp management because of its low sensitivity and predictive values relative to hysteroscopy, the possibility of inadequate sampling or missed malignant cells at the polyp base, and tissue fragmentation.

Consider the patient’s preference and the extent of pathology when choosing an outpatient or operating-room procedure; the authors state that precise polyp-based thresholds for that choice are unavailable.

For operating-room polypectomy, select resectoscope size and energy type according to the endometrial pathology and patient characteristics, including parity, difficulty with cervical dilation and cervical stenosis.
Hysterectomy is not considered first-line treatment for endometrial polyps despite preventing recurrence, because it entails high costs, complications and morbidity.
limitations: The authors state that estimates of polyp prevalence are constrained by a lack of studies focused on asymptomatic women.

They describe the evidence on malignant transformation as insufficient: available studies generally assess associations with cancer rather than the biological progression of a polyp, and the origin of malignant or premalignant tissue can be difficult to establish.
They state that evidence for medical treatment of endometrial polyps is limited.
They report insufficient evidence to replace post-removal histopathology with Doppler or power Doppler ultrasonography.
open_questions: The exact cause of endometrial polyps remains unknown.
Whether prevalence continues to rise or instead falls after menopause is unclear.
Whether diabetes primarily affects polyp growth or malignant degeneration is unclear.
The roles of sex hormones and hormone replacement therapy in polyp development remain disputed or uncertain.
Whether premalignant or malignant lesions arise within a polyp or in adjacent endometrium remains unresolved.
Whether polyp size affects neoplastic risk remains controversial.
A causal relationship between endometrial polyps and infertility has not been established.
The authors state that precise polyp characteristics defining when removal should occur in an outpatient rather than a surgical setting are unavailable.

The review describes associations between EP development and family history, age, diabetes, hypertension, obesity, hyperestrogenism, and Tamoxifen therapy. It also discusses genetic, inflammatory, hormonal, and iatrogenic contributions, while stating that the precise cause remains unknown.
EP are frequently asymptomatic. When symptoms occur, AUB is prominent; the review states that bleeding intensity does not depend on EP number, size, or location.

The review reports altered inflammatory mediators and factors related to endometrial receptivity in women with EP, but does not establish that EP cause infertility. It attributes improved clinical pregnancy rates after hysteroscopic polipectomy before ARTs to a cited systematic review.

Hysterosonography is described as more capable than conventional TUS of detecting small EP and characterizing their position and size. The review reports diagnostic sensitivity and specificity similar to hysteroscopy, while noting that hysterosonography cannot provide definitive histopathology or treatment.

Power Doppler may help raise suspicion of malignancy from vascular patterns, but the review finds insufficient support for using Doppler or power Doppler in place of histopathological examination after EP removal.
The authors say expectant management can be considered for asymptomatic premenopausal patients with small EP and low endometrial cancer risk, with counseling about the potential cancer risk.

The review describes a limited role for medical EP management. It attributes prevention of EP during LNGIUS use to a cited study and describes a possible preventive role for hormonal treatments with strong antiestrogenic activity.

Office polypectomy is described as less costly and associated with lower intraoperative risk than operating-room treatment. The review reports no precise polyp-characteristic limits for choosing between these settings.
The review states that hysterectomy prevents recurrence of polypoid lesions but is not considered first-line EP treatment because of its costs, complications, and morbidity.

document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: This review aims to update the literature on the pathophysiology, natural history, diagnosis, and treatment of endometrial polyps (EPs). EPs are localized, sessile or pedunculated protrusions of the endometrial lining formed by excess growth of glands and stroma around a vascular core. They are described as the most common intrauterine disease and may affect up to 34.9% of women during their lifetime. Their size, site, histopathology, course, and presentation vary. They occur in women with infertility, including up to 32% of patients undergoing in-vitro-fertilization, and malignant transformation occurs in about 3.1% of patients. Trans-vaginal ultrasound has sensitivity of 91% and specificity of 90% for EPs. Hysteroscopy is the current diagnostic gold standard because it permits direct assessment of size and morphology. It also permits excision, with incomplete removal reported in about 1.9% of inpatient procedures and 4.3% of outpatient procedures. Recurrence varies with individual risk factors, ranging between 2.5% and 43.6%. Other management options may be considered individually. The authors intend the review to help clinicians update their knowledge of EP management.

document_sections.heading: 1. Introduction
document_sections.content: Endometrial polyps (EP) are localized endometrial protrusions, either sessile or pedunculated, produced by hyperplastic growth of glands and stroma around a vascular core. Most are benign, although atypical hyperplasia or endometrial carcinoma can be present in 3.8% of postmenopausal patients. Abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) is the principal manifestation and is reported in 3.7–65% of patients with EP. Other polyps are found incidentally during routine ultrasound in asymptomatic women. EPs may be associated with infertility and recurrent miscarriage in young women. The review aims to survey the literature on their pathophysiology, natural history, diagnosis, and treatment.

document_sections.heading: 2. Classification
document_sections.content: The classification describes the macroscopic appearance and histopathological types of EP.

document_sections.heading: 2.1 Macroscopic Aspect
document_sections.content: EP may be sessile or pedunculated, single (80%) or multiple (20%), and differ in shape and diameter, from a few millimeters to centimeters. The usual appearance is one bulb-shaped pedunculated mass with a mean diameter equal to or less than 1 cm. Most originate in the uterine fundus (55.8%) or cornual mucosa (29.4%) and extend toward the internal cervical opening. Occasionally, they project beyond the external cervical orifice (ECO) and are visible during cervical examination.

document_sections.heading: 2.2 Histopathology
document_sections.content: EP mainly contain dense fibrous stroma and glands around a vascular core, beneath superficial epithelium; smooth muscle is present in some. The review distinguishes five categories. Hyperplastic polyps develop from the basal endometrium under estrogenic stimulation without progesterone opposition; they can coexist with endometrial hyperplasia and contain atypical areas, particularly after menopause. Atrophic polyps occur after menopause and result from regression of hyperplastic or functional polyps. Functional polyps show glandular changes resembling those of the surrounding endometrium and respond to hormonal changes during the menstrual cycle. Adenomatous polyps contain varying amounts of smooth muscle and fibrous muscle tissue; their “atypical” forms also have structural atypia and may be associated with malignant transformation. Pseudopolyps are small sessile lesions, generally smaller than 1 centimeter, that resemble adjacent endometrium, are detected only during the secretory phase, and may disappear after menstrual bleeding. Fig. 1 depicts hysteroscopic examples of a functional polyp in an infertile pre-menopausal woman, a cystic polyp during adjuvant tamoxifen therapy for breast cancer, and atypical and adenomatous polyps in post-menopausal women.

document_sections.heading: 2.2.1 Epidemiology
document_sections.content: The true population prevalence of EP is difficult to establish because studies focused on asymptomatic patients are lacking. Estimates range from 7.8% to 34.9%, depending on the population and individual risk factors. Reported prevalence is higher in postmenopausal women (11.8%) than in premenopausal women (5.8%) and reaches up to 32% among women considered for in-vitro-fertilization.

document_sections.heading: 2.2.2 Risk Factors
document_sections.content: Factors correlated with EP development include family history, age, diabetes, hypertension, obesity, hyperestrogenism, and Tamoxifen therapy. Chromosomal changes, including alterations of chromosomes 6 and 20, may contribute. Prevalence appears to rise with age during reproductive life, but its direction after menopause remains uncertain. Diabetes mellitus may increase EP risk, although whether it primarily affects polyp growth or malignant degeneration is unclear. Systemic hypertension, particularly with obesity, may be related to EP; advancing age is also associated with increased systolic pressure and hypertension prevalence. Relative or absolute estrogen excess is thought to increase EP risk. Obesity, early menarche, and late menopause, which entail greater estrogen exposure, are associated with higher EP prevalence. Tamoxifen users have also been reported to have increased risks of EP and endometrial cancer, probably because progesterone lacks antiproliferative activity on the endometrial mucosa in this setting.

document_sections.heading: 3. Pathogenesis
document_sections.content: Jovanovic et al. first demonstrated a monoclonal origin for EPs in hysterectomy specimens from 22 women in 1996. Their exact cause remains unknown. Histopathological diversity has led to a proposed multifactorial origin involving genetic, inflammatory, hormonal, and iatrogenic factors. Lynch and Cowden syndrome illustrate a possible genetic contribution; both are associated with increased risks of EP and endometrial cancer. Translocations and other abnormalities of chromosomes 6 and 12 have been described in women with EP and may alter endometrial architecture to produce polypoid structures. Rearrangements affecting the high mobility chromosomal proteins (HMGs) family also appear to contribute. Higher polyp prevalence after menopause has been associated with greater p63 expression in polyps and nearby endometrium. p53 has been identified as a marker of biological activity in postmenopausal EP, and some authors suggest that its overexpression in polyps may relate to increased endometrial cancer risk. p53 suppresses tumors by reducing expression of genes involved in proliferation and increasing expression of genes that prevent growth; it helps restrain inappropriate cell proliferation and maintain genomic integrity after genotoxic stress. Increased matrix metalloproteinase (MMPs) levels have been described in endometrial fluid from women with EP and other uterine conditions, including leiomyomas and adenomyosis. These proteins participate in angiogenesis, migration, proliferation, and cell death. Recent studies and a review report increased EP risk in women with chronic endometritis, supporting a possible inflammatory origin for some polyps. The contribution of estrogen and progesterone remains debated. Some authors speculate that increased aromatase expression and sexual hormone receptors produce elongation of endometrial glands, stromal tissue, and spiral arteries characteristic of EP. The effect of hormone replacement therapy on EP development is controversial, whereas a levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine device appears protective.

document_sections.heading: 4. Natural History
document_sections.content: EP may regress, remain stable, grow, or undergo malignant transformation. Spontaneous regression depends mainly on size, with larger polyps less likely to regress. A cited recent study reported regression of 26.7% after 1 year follow-up for EP with a mean diameter of 10.7 mm; regression was substantially lower for EP with a mean diameter of 15.1 mm. The comparison is printed as mean difference, 4.4; 95% confidence interval (CI), 0.2–8.6; p = 5.04. A cited prospective study likewise found that polyps bigger than 1 cm tended to persist and cause AUB compared with those smaller than 1 cm. Regression may coincide with one or more episodes of menorrhagia and mild/moderate pelvic pain.

document_sections.heading: 5. Risk of Malignancy
document_sections.content: Most EP are benign, but a reported proportion ranging from 0% to 12.9% may develop premalignant or malignant lesions. Robust evidence about this progression is lacking: it is difficult to determine whether such lesions arise within the polyp or begin in adjacent endometrium and involve the polyp later, and published research has generally examined associations with cancer rather than the biological evolution of individual polyps. A cited prospective controlled study of 248 women with AUB, with or without EP, found endometrial hyperplasia more often in women with polyps but found no between-group difference in malignancy. In a cited multicenter study of 1922 women, Ferrazzi et al. reported atypical hyperplastic polyps in 1.2% of asymptomatic and 2.2% of symptomatic postmenopausal patients (p < 0.005). A cited systematic review of 9266 women estimated pooled prevalence of endometrial cancer confined to EP at 3.1%, with rates of 1.12% in premenopausal women and 4.93% in post-menopausal women. Among postmenopausal patients alone (2586 women), reported prevalences of premalignant and malignant lesions were 1.8% and 2.3%, respectively. In patients diagnosed with EP, stated endometrial cancer risk factors are advanced age (>60 years), postmenopausal status, AUB history, Tamoxifen therapy, obesity, hypertension, and diabetes. A cited systematic review and meta-analysis identified postmenopausal status and AUB as major predictors, with relative risk (RR) of 3.86 (95% CI 2.92–5.11) and 1.97 (95% CI 1.24–3.15), respectively. Whether polyp size affects neoplastic risk remains disputed: some authors report no effect, whereas others associate diameters greater than 15 and 18 mm with atypical histology. Supporting the former view, a cited retrospective study of 1467 patients with EP found endometrial cancer in 8.5% (n = 125); among those cancers, 10.4% were confined to EP and 89.6% involved both EP and adjacent endometrium. Endometrial cancer was less frequent among women with EP than among those with uterine fibroids (11.7%). Those study authors concluded that EP were incidental findings accompanying endometrial cancer rather than its precursors.

document_sections.heading: 6. Clinical Presentation
document_sections.content: Most EP are asymptomatic and are detected incidentally on routine ultrasound or during assessment of infertile couples. Symptomatic polyps are associated with AUB, but bleeding intensity does not depend on polyp number, size, or location. Large polyps can protrude through the external cervical orifice (ECO) and become apparent on routine gynecological examination. During reproductive life, intermenstrual bleeding is the most common complaint; EP are found in 10% to 40% of women with premenopausal bleeding. Postmenopausal uterine bleeding can occur with or without hormone replacement therapy. EP occur in about 15–25% of infertile women, although a causal link with infertility is not established. Local factors associated with EP may impair sperm migration and endometrial receptivity. Studies report increased inflammatory cytokines and Glycodelin, an endometrial glycoprotein that inhibits natural killer cell function, alongside reduced expression of implantation mediators tumor necrosis factor (TNFa) and Insulin-like Growth Factor Binding Protein 1 (IGFBP-1). A cited systematic review found that hysteroscopic polipectomy before ARTs can improve clinical pregnancy rates in women with infertility.

document_sections.heading: 7. Diagnosis
document_sections.content: On physical examination, only prolapsed EP can be seen as globular, friable, pedunculated structures extending through the external cervical orifice; this appearance more commonly represents a cervical polyp. Transvaginal Ultrasound (TUS) is frequently used and is described as cost-effective, with mean sensitivity of 91%, specificity of 90%, positive predictive value (PPV) of 86%, and negative predictive value (NPV) of 90%. EP generally appear as hyperechogenic lesions with regular margins in the uterine cavity along the endometrial line. Associated cystic spaces correspond to dilated glands containing proteinaceous material. These features are nonspecific and can resemble submucosal leiomyomas, endometrial hyperplasia, or endometrial cancer. Studies of Power Doppler found low specificity for differentiation of polyps, hyperplasia, and cancer when using vascular resistance index, pulsatility, and polyp size. Power Doppler performed better at distinguishing the single-vessel pattern typical of polyps from the multiple diffuse vessels of hyperplastic and neoplastic endometrial lesions. It may raise suspicion of malignancy but cannot reliably distinguish other conditions, including endometrial hyperplasia and submucosal myomas. Evidence is insufficient to replace histopathological assessment after polyp removal with Doppler or power doppler ultrasonography. Hysterosonography uses saline infusion to distend the uterine cavity, improving EP detection; it is described as safe, well tolerated, and minimally invasive. Relative to conventional TUS, it better identifies smaller lesions and characterizes their site and size. Its reported sensitivity and specificity are similar to those of hysteroscopy, and it permits simultaneous assessment of other pelvic structures, but it cannot provide definitive anatomopathological diagnosis or treatment. Diagnostic hysteroscopy is considered the gold standard, with sensitivity of 90%, specificity of 93%, PPV of 96%, and VPN of 93%. Direct endometrial inspection improves polyp characterization and permits outpatient “see and treat” management. Office polipectomy is described as effective and able to provide definitive histopathological diagnosis in one procedural step; compared with traditional resectoscopic surgery, office hysteroscopy is cheaper, safer, and does not require hospital admission or analgesia. Endoscopic assessment should document polyp number; size, estimated against open Grasping 5-French forceps with a diameter of 6 mm; location and relation to the tubal ostium; soft, friable, dense, or semi-myomatous texture; sessile or pediculated implantation; surface vessels; and coexisting myomas, adenomyosis, or Mullerian abnormalities. Abundant tortuous surface vessels are the most relevant hysteroscopic sign raising suspicion of malignancy. Blind biopsy or curettage is currently discouraged for EP management: relative to hysteroscopy, its sensitivity is 10%, PPV 66%, and NPV 33%. Blind sampling may fail to obtain adequate polyp tissue or miss malignant cells at its base, while tissue fragmentation may hinder histopathological examination.

document_sections.heading: 8. Differential Diagnosis
document_sections.content: EP should be distinguished from other uterine disorders, including intracavitary leiomyomas, endometrial hyperplasia, and endometrial cancer.

document_sections.heading: 9. Treatment
document_sections.content: Management should be selected after assessing the patient's history, including pregnancy intentions, symptoms, malignancy risk factors, and the physician's technical qualifications. The options presented are conservative nonsurgical care, conservative surgery, and radical surgery. An expectant “wait and see” approach can be considered for asymptomatic premenopausal patients with small EP (≤1 cm) and low endometrial carcinoma risk. In such patients, spontaneous regression may occur in 26.7% of cases after 1 year follow-up. According to AAGL guidelines, expectant management should follow counseling about possible endometrial carcinoma risk. Evidence for medical management is limited. WadaHiraike et al. reported that intermittent oral contraceptives (OC) for 2–5 months (median 3 months) produced greater regression of sessile than pedunculated polyps (76% vs. 44%), suggesting greater OC sensitivity in sessile lesions. Possible contributors to regression include OC-related proapoptotic effects and progesterone-related anti-inflammatory effects, with gradual flattening of endometrial protrusions. Certain hormonal treatments, particularly progestogen with strong antiestrogenic activity, may help prevent polyp formation. Gardner et al. reported prevention of EP in women using levonorgestrel intrauterine system (LNGIUS). Hysteroscopic polipectomy is presented as a safe and effective conservative operation, providing symptom relief for 75 to 100% of patients. It can take place in an outpatient clinic or operating room. Outpatient removal is associated with lower intraoperative risks and better cost-effectiveness; operating-room polypectomy has a considerably greater risk of uterine perforation and penetration than office hysteroscopy. For office removal, polyps less than 0.5 cm can be excised with 5-Fr mechanical instruments such as scissors or grasping forceps. Laser or a 5-Fr bipolar electrode can make precise cuts more quickly than mechanical instruments. The 15-Fr bipolar office resectoscope enables treatment of multiple polyps and EP larger than 3 centimeters in less time. Smaller tissue removal devices (TRD), also termed “hysteroscopic morcellators”, may decrease pain and procedure duration by combining cutting and aspiration, thereby reducing repeated passage of instruments through the cervix. TRD use a disposable rigid inner metal cutting tube that rotates and/or reciprocates within an outer tube of variable diameter (9 to 4 mm), avoiding thermal injury to excised tissue. Their learning curve is short and is aided by computer simulators. No precise polyp-characteristic thresholds currently determine whether removal should occur in the office or operating room; reluctance toward outpatient care or extensive pathology may favor surgery in the latter setting. Endometrial pathology and patient characteristics, including parity, difficulty with cervical dilation, and cervical stenosis, should guide selection of resectoscope size (15 Fr, 22 Fr, 26 Fr or 27 Fr) and energy type (monopolar or bipolar). Several studies report shorter operations and a shorter learning curve with TRD than with a standard resectoscope. After complete excision, recurrence is reported in approximately 2.5% to 43.6% of cases; previous polypectomies, multiple polyps, and endometriosis are associated with increased recurrence risk. Hysterectomy prevents recurrence of polypoid lesions but entails high costs, complications, and morbidity, so it is not currently considered first-line EP therapy. Fig. 2 presents an algorithm based on the authors’ experience that uses trans-vaginal ultrasound with or without diagnostic hysteroscopy to diagnose polyps and identifies obesity, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, tamoxifen therapy, and additional ultrasound or hysteroscopy findings as endometrial cancer risk factors.
